To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
international patent laws pose monetary, logistical and political barriers to access of the most current and most effective treatments to HIV/AIDS patients in developing countries.
international trade agreements and the resulting patent laws have a significant impact on the ability of developing countries to access medications.

the flexibilities of the TRIPS agreement have been implemented by the countries of Brazil, India and China to varying degrees of success, and that these countries have had to make difficult policy decisions regarding the implementation of these flexibilities in the face of international trade agreements and their own domestic needs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the international trade regime and patent law affects the access to HIV/AIDS medications in developing countries.
the impact of TRIPS on the ability of developing countries to access the latest HIV/AIDS medications and how the flexibilities within TRIPS have been implemented in practice.
the impact of the international trade and patent system on developing countries' abilities to access HIV/AIDS medications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the TRIPS Agreement and its flexibilities are not adequate to ensure the right to health in developing countries, especially in the context of HIV/AIDS.
international trade and patent laws have a significant impact in limiting the ability of developing countries to access HIV medications.
the flexibilities in TRIPS are not adequate enough to provide access to the most current and advanced HIV medications to the developing countries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the WTO and TRIPS are not the most efficient means to achieve universal access to medications.
TRIPS has not been able to achieve the goals it was created for and that the flexibilities that have been created to help with access are not sufficient to reach the goal of the right to health.
TRIPS is a flawed international patent law, but it is the only one in existence and is a necessary step towards a more comprehensive right to health.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the international community must continue to work to improve access to HIV/AIDS medications and treatment.
there is a need for greater access to HIV/AIDS treatment and a need for greater flexibility to achieve this.
the current patent system in place does not adequately provide for the health of the people.
